title: The RBI Just Handed India's Government Its Biggest Cheque Ever. Here's Why It Matters.
excerpt: A record ₹2.87 lakh crore dividend — earned largely from defending the rupee during the Iran war — has compressed India's fiscal deficit to just 9.6% of the full-year target in two months. But the real test lies ahead.
body:
India's fiscal deficit in the first two months of the current financial year has landed at a figure that caught even seasoned economists off guard — just 9.6% of the government's full-year target of ₹16.96 lakh crore.

The number, released by the Controller General of Accounts on Tuesday, marks a dramatic compression from April, when the deficit had already ballooned to 21.4% of the budget estimate. The turnaround has a single, unmistakable driver: a record ₹2.87 lakh crore dividend from the Reserve Bank of India, the largest surplus transfer in the central bank's history.

## The RBI's War-Time Windfall

The RBI's record payout didn't happen by accident. The central bank's gross income surged 26.4% in FY26, powered largely by a 52% jump in gains from foreign exchange transactions — ₹1.69 lakh crore worth of profits realised as the RBI sold dollars from its reserves to defend the rupee during the Iran war-induced turbulence.

Interest income from foreign securities, primarily US Treasuries, added another ₹1.07 lakh crore. Together with a 20.6% expansion in its balance sheet to nearly ₹92 lakh crore, the RBI's war-year earnings handed the government a lifeline just when it needed one most.

Governor Sanjay Malhotra's board approved the transfer after setting aside ₹1.09 lakh crore for the Contingent Risk Buffer — more than double last year's provision — maintaining the buffer at 6.5% of the balance sheet. The caution is deliberate: in an era of volatile capital flows and geopolitical shocks, the central bank is building a bigger cushion even as it writes a bigger cheque.



> **"The number, released by the Controller General of Accounts on Tuesday, marks a dramatic compression from April, when the deficit had already ballooned to 21.4% of the budget estimate."**


## The Excise Duty Hole

The fiscal relief is welcome because the government's tax revenue engine is running rough. Net tax receipts in April-May stood at ₹3.48 lakh crore — essentially flat compared to the same period last year, despite an economy that grew 6.5% in real terms.

The culprit is self-inflicted but politically necessary: in March, the Centre slashed excise duties on petrol and diesel by ₹10 per litre each to shield consumers from surging global crude prices. That decision is now costing the exchequer roughly ₹14,000 crore every month. Excise duty collections have contracted 20% year-on-year in the first two months.

Income tax receipts, meanwhile, grew a sluggish 6.8% — well below the 17.7% annual growth rate the budget assumed. The gap will need to close sharply in the second half if the government is to meet its 4.3% fiscal deficit target without resorting to additional borrowing.

On the spending side, the government has been anything but cautious. Total expenditure surged 18% to ₹8.81 lakh crore, with capital expenditure — spending on roads, railways and physical infrastructure — climbing 13.4% to ₹2.51 lakh crore. Revenue expenditure rose even faster at 20.1%, driven by ballooning subsidies and interest payments.

## Oil Prices Change the Calculus

What makes this moment different from the anxiety of two months ago is what has happened to oil. Brent crude, which peaked above $126 per barrel in April during the worst of the Iran conflict, has crashed to around $71 — a 43% decline that is still accelerating as US-Iran talks in Doha show "positive progress" and tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz gradually recovers.

For India, which imports nearly 90% of its crude requirements, every dollar off the oil price translates directly into savings on the subsidy bill, the import bill and the current account deficit. ICRA Chief Economist Aditi Nayar now expects only a "marginal overshooting" of the fiscal deficit target, down from a previous estimate of a 40 basis-point slippage.

Goldman Sachs has followed suit, raising India's 2026 growth forecast by 30 basis points while lowering its inflation projection, calling for a balance of payments surplus of 0.7% of GDP.

## The Diaspora Angle

For NRIs watching from abroad, India's fiscal discipline has direct implications. A government that stays within its borrowing limits keeps bond yields stable, the rupee less volatile and the investment climate predictable. The record RBI dividend, ironically earned from defending the rupee against the very shocks NRIs feared, has given the government breathing room to maintain its infrastructure spending — the capital expenditure that underpins everything from highways to smart cities to manufacturing hubs.

The risk, as Kotak Mahindra Bank's chief economist Upasna Bhardwaj noted, is that the RBI dividend was "marginally lower than expected" and may not fully neutralise the subsidy pressures ahead. If oil rebounds or the monsoon disappoints, the fiscal cushion could thin quickly.

But for now, two months into a fiscal year that began under the shadow of war, India's books look better than almost anyone predicted.

*Sources: Controller General of Accounts, Reserve Bank of India Annual Report FY26, Reuters, Mint, ICRA, Goldman Sachs Research*
